Even after files have been added to the source-controlled project, other developers will not be able to work with them. Developers will be able to manually use their source control system to check files out and in if they need to, but the added files will not be displayed in the Project Manager for any developer except the developer who added the files. To make the files available to other developers, update the project list.

When you update the project list, [[T0]]:
 - Generates a new local project file list (.pjm file).
- Checks in the new project file list (with the option set to keep the file checked out).
- Merges the local and central project file lists if there are differences. If a merge conflict occurs, [[T1]] displays a dialog box to help you resolve the merge conflicts.
- Rebuilds the local project (.pjx) file based on the merged project file list.
- Gets local copies of files added to the project by other developers.
- Prompts you to get the latest versions of the project files.
- Refreshes the display in the Project Manager to reflect changes.

- From the Project menu, choose Source Control , and then choose Update Project List .

As part of the update procedures, [[T0]] prompts you to get the latest versions of files. If you have a file already checked out, as a general rule you shouldn't get the latest version, because your version is almost certainly more current than the one on the network.

If you're getting the latest version of a text file (such as a program), the source control software can attempt to merge the latest changes with your version. For more information about merging text files, see How to: Check In Files.

When you're finished, other developers should also then update their project list (using the same procedure) in order to be able to work with the files you've added.

Establishing a connection uses time and memory on both the client and the server. When you optimize connections, you balance your need for high performance against the resource requirements of your application.

The number of connections used by [[T0]] depends on whether you force the closing of unused connections, and how you set the length of the connection idle timeout.

You can use connections exclusively or share a connection. Each method has its benefits. When you use a connection exclusively, your application experiences no contentions for connection resources once a connection is established. If each result set uses an exclusive connection, you can also intermingle asynchronous processing on multiple result sets.

When you use a shared connection, you have one connection for multiple result sets. You must serialize data manipulation operations on the result sets sharing the same connection, and design the application to test the connection for busyness any time conflicts might occur. For information on sharing a connection, see How to: Share Connections for Multiple Remote Views.

If your application doesn't take any action for a long time, you can reduce connection use by setting the IdleTimeout property on the connection. The IdleTimeout property controls the interval of time connections are allowed to idle before they're closed by [[T0]]. By default, connections wait indefinitely and are not deactivated until specifically closed by the user.

You set the idle time for a connection definition with the IdleTimeout property of the [[T1]] Function function; you can set the IdleTimeout property for an active connection with the [[T2]] Function function.

[[T3]] closes connections even if Browse windows and forms displaying remote data are still open, and then automatically reconnects when the connection is needed again. However, [[T4]] cannot close a connection if:
 - Results of a query from the server are pending.
- The connection is in manual transaction mode. You must commit or roll back the transaction and switch to automatic transaction mode before the connection can be closed.

You set the transaction mode for a connection definition with the Transactions property of the [[T5]] function; you can set the transaction mode for an active connection with the [[T6]] function.

You can improve performance by closing connections that your application is no longer using. Connections are closed automatically for you when you close a view. If the connection is shared by multiple views, [[T0]] closes the connection when the last view using the connection is closed.

You can control the connection for a query manually if you don't want to update the data in a cursor. Use a [[T1]] pass-through query to select the data you need into a local cursor and then close the connection.

When you create .dbf files, [[T0]] automatically gives them code page marks so that you can tell which code pages they use. However, if you use .dbf files from previous versions of [[T1]], they might not have code page marks.

You can determine whether a .dbf file has a code page mark by using the [[T2]] Function function after opening the file or by having [[T3]] check when you open the file.

- From the Tools menu, choose Options .
- Select the Data tab.
- Set the Prompt for code page check box, if it's not already set. To save this setting for future sessions of [[T0]], choose Set as Default . Tip Instead of setting the Prompt for code page check box, you can use the [[T1]] command to check for code pages.

If a file doesn't have a code page mark, you must add a mark, as described in the following section.

If you use a .dbf file from a previous version of [[T0]], the file might not have a code page mark; without such a mark, the file might not display properly. If automatic code page checking is enabled, when you open the file you can tell if it has a code page mark. If it doesn't have one, you can add one.

- Ensure automatic code page checking is in effect (see the previous procedure).
- Open the file. If the file doesn't have a code page mark, the Code Page dialog box appears.
- Choose the appropriate code page.
- View the file to see if you assigned the proper code page. If you can't see some of the data, or if you can't recognize some of it, the code page is not correct.
- If the code page is incorrect, remove the code page mark by using the [[T0]] program in the [[T1]] Tools\Cpzero directory.
- Repeat this procedure until the code page is correct. Note Text files such as program (.prg) and query (.qpr) files don't have code page marks. This means that you can't tell which code pages the files use. However, if you include such files in a project, the project can keep a record of the code pages used. For more information, see How to: Specify the Code Page of a Text File .

If a .dbf file doesn't display properly, it might have the wrong code page mark. You can remove the code page mark with the [[T0]] program located in Tools\Cpzero. Running [[T1]] sets the code page to 0, meaning none.

- Run [[T0]] using the following syntax: [[T1]] " filename ", 0 Note When you remove the code page mark of a .dbf file, the data in the file doesn't change. To change the code page of the data, you must mark the file with the proper code page.
You can change the code page of a .dbf file by removing its code page mark and then adding a new one, by copying the file to another file, or by using the [[T0]] program.

- Use the [[T0]] command, specifying the target code page with the [[T1]] clause. (To set the code page to the current system code page, omit the [[T2]] clause.) For example, to copy [[T3]] to [[T4]], while changing the code page to 866, use the following commands: [[T5]].[[T6]].[[T7]] 866

When the [[T8]] completes, the data in the resulting file will have the new code page.

- Run [[T0]] using the following syntax: [[T1]] " filename ", [[T2]] Note Some characters cannot be translated between code pages successfully. In addition, [[T3]] doesn't support some code page translations. Always check the results of a code page change to be sure that your data has been translated successfully.
